thesis: Check a test design against the method, then look past the test.

picks.title: Measuring Ad Effectiveness Using Geo Experiments
picks.author: Jon Vaver, Jim Koehler
picks.why: The method paper behind most geo-holdout tooling. Hold a test plan against it: assignment of regions, pre-period, test period, and how the incremental return and its confidence interval are built.
lookFor: How do they use the pre-test period to reduce variance, and how long does it need to be?
What does the paper imply about the number of regions and the size of the spend change needed to see an effect within a few weeks?
How do they treat carryover after the test ends, and do you need a cooldown window?
picks.gist: Google's description of geo experiments: non-overlapping regions are randomly assigned to treatment or control and served through geo-targeted ads, which gives results that translate directly into bidding and budget decisions. The follow-on Trimmed Match work deals with a small number of very different regions.
picks.holds: Still the base design behind current geo-testing tools. Later work such as Trimmed Match refines the estimator for few, uneven regions. The design logic is unchanged.

picks.title: Season 7, Episode 26: Demystifying open source MMM (with Michael Kaminsky)
picks.author: Eric Seufert, Michael Kaminsky
picks.why: It answers what comes after a geo test. Kaminsky is candid about when marketing mix modelling is overkill, when last-touch is good enough for a smaller advertiser, and why experiments should come before models. That bears on how much measurement infrastructure is worth buying. He sells MMM software, so weigh his view of the alternatives.
lookFor: What are his criteria for when a business is ready for a mix model, and when experiments plus last-touch are enough?
How does he validate a model, and could a geo test serve as the calibration point?
Which marketing data science work can a small team now do in-house?
picks.gist: Seufert and Kaminsky discuss the open-source mix modelling tools and the accusations of bias against them, how to judge a model through parameter recovery and forecast accuracy, and when simple attribution beats complex modelling for smaller advertisers. Kaminsky calls incrementality testing the gold standard and recommends geo-level tests before building a model.

practice.title: What does one point of interest do to a company priced at 25 times earnings?
practice.prompt: No calculator app, no search. Long-term interest rates rise by one percentage point. Estimate how much value a company trading at 25 times earnings loses, all else equal. Then do it again for one at 50 times earnings. Write down the formula you are assuming before you calculate, and say in one sentence why the two answers differ.
practice.reveal:
One route, with the simplest model: price over earnings is roughly 1 divided by (required return minus growth).

- 25 times earnings implies a gap of 4 points. One point more makes it 5, so 20 times earnings: about 20% lower.
- 50 times earnings implies a gap of 2 points. One point more makes it 3, so about 33 times: about a third lower.

The second company loses more because more of its value sits far in the future, and distant cash flows are the most sensitive to the discount rate. That is the same idea as duration in bonds. The model ignores that higher rates often come with higher growth or inflation, which is the first thing to challenge in your own answer.
